routes.description: Establish the nature and commands of God as a unified foundation for objective moral value and obligation, then show that this account explains the relevant moral phenomena with fewer or less serious foundational difficulties than godless normative realism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if divine nature supplies a nonarbitrary standard of goodness, divine authority constitutes universally applicable duties, and the resulting account retains a comparative explanatory advantage over irreducible godless normativity.

motionBridge.description: Connect God's necessarily good nature and authoritative commands to a comparatively adequate account of both objective moral values and objective duties.

centralBridges.description: Explain why God's essential nature can constitute the paradigm of moral goodness without appealing to an independent moral standard.
Explain how commands consistent with God's nature generate genuine obligations while allowing derivative principles and morally relevant circumstances to govern particular cases.
Show that the rival account's irreducible moral entities and natural-to-moral relations lack sufficient metaphysical or explanatory support.
Preserve responsible agency and moral knowledge under the theistic account while identifying whether the rival naturalistic setting can support both.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for how divine moral requirements bind agents who do not explicitly identify God as their source, including difficult cases of impaired moral understanding.
Explain the role of general divine commands in responsibility, recognition of wrongdoing, and accountability despite anticipated disobedience.

routes.description: Establish irreducible normative facts and morally relevant nondivine features as sufficient grounds for objective value and obligation, then show that appeals to God neither uniquely explain those facts nor avoid comparable explanatory stopping points.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if godless normative realism accounts for objective goodness, duties, agency, and moral knowledge while the proposed theistic foundation proves unnecessary or rests on equally basic normative assumptions.

motionBridge.description: Connect irreducible moral facts and morally relevant features of situations to a complete, nondivine account of objective moral values and duties.

centralBridges.description: Explain how intrinsic values and irreducible normative relations can be basic features of reality and can ground obligations without divine commands.
Show that suffering, promises, capacities, and other morally relevant facts can generate duties without requiring an additional divine order.
Establish that theistic grounding also terminates in normative assumptions or unexplained relations, preventing obscurity objections from yielding a comparative advantage.
Provide a godless account compatible with responsible mental causation and justified confidence in evolved cognitive and moral faculties.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether commands can bind agents who do not apprehend their source or authority and whether the theory treats impaired agents consistently.
Determine whether divine commands add a necessary normative function beyond communicating existing good and evil, especially when disobedience is anticipated.

sections.title: Ultimate Ground of Moral Value
sections.rationale: The competing accounts must identify what makes goodness and badness objective: God's essential nature or irreducible normative features. This issue also tests whether either proposed standard imports an unexplained normative premise.

sections.title: Constitution and Scope of Objective Duty
sections.rationale: The motion expressly includes duties, making the dispute between authoritative divine commands and obligations generated by morally relevant nondivine facts a principal burden for both sides.

sections.title: Metaphysical Relations and Explanatory Ultimates
sections.rationale: Both routes depend on foundational relations linking their proposed grounds to moral facts. The comparative burden includes ontology, causal or constitutive intelligibility, theoretical economy, and the legitimacy of explanatory stopping points.

sections.title: Universality, Accountability, and the Purpose of Commands
sections.rationale: An account of duty must explain who is bound, how authority reaches unaware or impaired agents, why commands are needed, and how wrongdoing and accountability arise when commands are violated.

sections.title: Moral Agency and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: Objective duties require agents capable of responsible action, while objective moral claims require defensible epistemic access. The rival accounts therefore must support freedom, mental efficacy, and reliable moral cognition.
